name: Campbell's Law
statement: The more any quantitative social indicator is used for social decision-making, the more subject it will be to corruption pressures and the more apt it will be to distort and corrupt the social processes it is intended to monitor.
statementAccent: the more subject it will be to corruption pressures
meaning: The harder a society leans on one number to make its decisions, the more that number gets gamed — and the more the activity behind it bends out of shape to feed it.
mechanism: Any high-stakes indicator invites two responses: improve the reality it tracks, or improve the indicator directly. The second is usually faster and safer for the individual, so under enough pressure the indicator and the reality drift apart — and the indicator, now corrupted, distorts the very process it was meant to monitor.

examples.text: In the Atlanta Public Schools scandal, a 2011 state investigation found educators at dozens of schools had erased and corrected pupils' answers on standardized tests; in 2015, eleven were convicted under Georgia's racketeering statute. Tie careers and funding to a test score and the score rises — sometimes by altering the answer sheets.

New York's CompStat policing model has been repeatedly accused of 'juking the stats': downgrading felonies to lesser offences so the numbers improve. The measured crime rate falls while the streets do not — the classic Campbell distortion.

Chasing the U.S. News rankings, Temple University's business school submitted false data for years and its dean was convicted of fraud; Columbia was stripped of its ranking in 2022 after a professor exposed inflated figures. The ranking became the target, and the data feeding it decayed.

whyItMatters: This is the sharper, more institutional cousin of Goodhart's Law: it predicts not just a bad metric but real damage to the thing being measured. Wherever a single indicator carries high stakes — test scores, crime statistics, hospital waiting times — expect both the gaming and the collateral distortion, and design the stakes accordingly.

working.lead: Never hang everything on one number
working.text: the corruption pressure scales with the stakes on a single indicator; spread the weight across several and no one of them is worth gaming.
watch indicators to learn what is happening without attaching consequences to them, so at least some stay honest.
independent verification of the numbers — the response Temple built after its scandal — is what catches the gaming a trusted metric hides.

working.lead: Distinguish real gains from gamed ones
working.text: some improvement under a target is genuine; ask whether the underlying process actually got better, not just the number.

limits: Campbell's Law is a directional tendency, not a theorem — it predicts pressure and likelihood, not certainty, and the effect scales with the stakes, so low-stakes monitoring indicators are far less prone to distortion. It does not claim measurement itself is bad or argue for abandoning metrics; auditing, multiple indicators, and verification units genuinely mitigate it. And not every gain under a target is gaming — sometimes the number improves because the reality did (England's A&E waiting times really did fall under the four-hour target, even as some hospitals gamed it). Separating true improvement from distortion is itself case-specific and contested.
misreadings: Campbell's Law is often collapsed into Goodhart's, but its claim is sharper: it is specifically about social decision-making, and it warns that the distortion damages the underlying social process, not merely the number. It does not say indicators are useless — only that the more weight one carries, the less it can be trusted.
origin: The social psychologist Donald T. Campbell set it out in "Assessing the Impact of Planned Social Change", where he introduced it as one of two "pessimistic laws". The paper had a tangled publication history that citations often garble: a version was presented at a conference in Visegrád, Hungary in May 1974; it was published in 1975 as a chapter in Gene M. Lyons's Social Research and Public Policies (Public Affairs Center, Dartmouth College); it was reprinted in December 1976, with Dartmouth's permission, as Paper #8 in the Occasional Paper Series of the Evaluation Center at Western Michigan University; and it reached its widest audience when Evaluation and Program Planning ran it in 1979. Campbell and the economist Charles Goodhart arrived at parallel conclusions independently, from social science and monetary policy respectively.
